title: Chili pepper
description: Varieties of pepper of the genus ''Capsicum''
wiki_lead:
Chili peppers, also spelled chile or chilli (from Classical Nahuatl  chīlli [ˈt͡ʃiːlːi] ), are varieties of berry-fruit plants from the genus Capsicum, which are members of the nightshade family Solanaceae, cultivated for their pungency (spicy heat). They are used as a spice to add pungency in many cuisines. Capsaicin and the related capsaicinoids give chili peppers their intensity when ingested or applied topically. Chili peppers exhibit a range of heat and flavors. This diversity is the reason behind the availability of different types of chili powder, each offering its own taste and heat level.
Chili peppers originated in Central or South America and were first cultivated in Mexico. European explorers brought chili peppers back to the Old World in the late 15th century as part of the Columbian exchange, which led to the cultivation of multiple varieties across the world for food and traditional medicine. Five Capsicum species have been widely cultivated: annuum, baccatum, chinense, frutescens, and pubescens.

Chili peppers originated in Central or South America and were first cultivated in Mexico. European explorers brought chili peppers back to the Old World in the late 15th century as part of the Columbian exchange, which led to the cultivation of multiple varieties across the world for food and traditional medicine. Five Capsicum species have been widely cultivated: annuum, baccatum, chinense, frutescens, and pubescens.


History


Origins
Capsicum plants originated in modern-day Peru and Bolivia, and have been a part of human diets since about 7,500 BC. They are one of the oldest cultivated crops in the Americas. Chili peppers were cultivated in east-central Mexico some 6,000 to 9,000 years ago, and independently across different locations in the Americas including highland Peru and Bolivia, central Mexico, and the Amazon. They were among the first self-pollinating crops cultivated in those areas.
Peru has the highest diversity of cultivated Capsicum; it is a center of diversification where varieties of all five domesticates were introduced, grown, and consumed in pre-Columbian times. The largest diversity of wild Capsicum peppers is consumed in Bolivia. Bolivian consumers distinguish two basic forms: ulupicas, species with small round fruits including C. eximium, C. cardenasii, C. eshbaughii, and C. caballeroi landraces; and arivivis with small elongated fruits including C. baccatum var. baccatum and C. chacoense varieties.


Etymology
The English word is from Classical Nahuatl  chīlli with the same meaning. The name of the plant is unrelated to that of the country Chile. While pepper originally meant the genus Piper, not Capsicum, the Oxford English Dictionary and  Merriam-Webster record both usages. The three primary spellings are chili (common in North America), chile (Central America and parts of the US) and chilli (United Kingdom and former British colonies). The specific dish name "chili con carne" is normally written with one "l" in both American and British English.


Distribution to Europe

In 1493, Diego Álvarez Chanca accompanied Christopher Columbus on his second voyage to the West Indies. Upon returning to Spain with chili peppers, Chanca became the first European to document their medicinal uses in the Old World, publishing his observations in 1494. Columbus and his crew called the Capsicum fruits "peppers" (pimientos in Spanish) because they were pungent like black pepper (Piper nigrum). The introduction of chilies to Europe formed part of the wider interchange of plants, animals, and cultures between the New World and the Old World known as the Columbian exchange. Unlike Piper vines, which grow naturally only in the tropics, chilies could be grown in temperate climates. By the mid-1500s, they had become a common garden plant in Spain and were incorporated into numerous dishes. By 1526, they had appeared in Italy, in 1543 in Germany, and by 1569 in the Balkans, where they came to be processed into paprika.


Distribution to the rest of the world

The rapid introduction of chilies to Africa and Asia was likely through Portuguese and Spanish traders in the 16th century, though the details are unrecorded. The Portuguese introduced them first to Africa and Arabia, and then to their colonies and trading posts in Asia, including Goa, Sri Lanka, and Malacca. grok_lead: The chili pepper (also spelled chile or chilli), despite commonly being called a "pepper," is not botanically related to true peppers of the genus Piper (such as black pepper); it is the fruit of plants belonging to the genus Capsicum within the nightshade family ( Solanaceae), native to Central and South America. These small to medium-sized berries vary in color from green to red, yellow, or purple when mature, and are characterized by their pungent heat derived from capsaicinoids, bioactive compounds concentrated in the placental tissue that produce a burning sensation by activating TRPV1 receptors in the mouth and digestive tract. Cultivated varieties range from mild sweet peppers like bell peppers ( C. annuum var. grossum) to intensely hot types such as habaneros ( C. chinense), with heat levels measured on the Scoville scale from 0 to over 2 million Scoville heat units (SHU). Originating as small, wild "berry-like" fruits in the lowlands of what is now Brazil around 10,000â15,000 years ago, chili peppers were domesticated in Mesoamerica by indigenous peoples as early as 10,000 years ago, with evidence from archaeological sites in Mexico showing their use in cooking, medicine, and rituals. Following Christopher Columbus's voyages in 1492, the plant was introduced to Europe in 1494, where it spread rapidly via Portuguese and Spanish trade routes to Asia, Africa, and beyond, transforming global cuisines and earning names like "barbarian pepper" in China due to its exotic origins. Today, chili peppers are grown in warm, frost-free climates worldwide, requiring well-drained soils, temperatures of 65â80Â°F (18â27Â°C), and full sun, with major production centered in tropical and subtropical regions. Global production of fresh and dried chilies and peppers reached approximately 37 million metric tons in 2022, led by China (about 45% of output), followed by Mexico, Indonesia, Turkey, and Spain, reflecting their staple role in diverse diets from Indian curries to Mexican salsas. Beyond culinary applications as spices, vegetables, and condimentsâwhere capsaicin enhances flavor and acts as a natural preservativeâchili peppers have medicinal uses, including pain relief in topical creams and potential benefits for metabolism and cardiovascular health, though high doses can cause gastrointestinal irritation. They also serve ornamental and cultural purposes, such as decorative ristras in the American Southwest believed to bring good luck.
